title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Coldwater hears data center details tonight while power, water and tax fights spread across Michigan.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy. Tonight Coldwater residents finally get their first public look at the proposed data centers, and the questions about power, water and tax breaks are front and center.
That's right, Emmy. The joint meeting between Coldwater City Council and planners is happening right now, giving folks a chance to hear the details before anything moves forward.
What exactly are residents pushing to learn at this session?
They're focused on how much electricity and water these projects would pull from local resources and what kind of tax incentives the companies are asking for.
That makes sense. These facilities can be massive, right? How does this fit into the bigger picture we've seen in other towns?

It's part of a wave of proposals hitting multiple communities at once. Similar concerns have already surfaced in nearby townships, with people worried about the strain on the grid and local water supplies.
And what about the farmland angle? A lot of these sites seem to go on agricultural land.
Exactly. Residents in Coldwater and surrounding areas are asking how much prime farmland might be taken out of production and what that means for the local economy long term.
Who are the main players here? Is it just the city council and one developer, or are there multiple companies involved?

It's the council and planners briefing everyone, but the projects tie into larger companies eyeing Michigan sites. Local officials are already fielding questions from residents about the scale and the deals on the table.
What happens if the community pushes back hard tonight?
The meeting is the starting point. Officials will take the feedback and decide how to move forward, whether that means adjusting plans, adding conditions or slowing things down.
We've seen power demand become a flashpoint elsewhere. How big could the electric bill impact be for regular ratepayers?
That's the core worry. A single large facility can pull hundreds of megawatts, and without new generation coming online fast enough, that load can push rates higher for everyone on the system.
Water is another big one. How are towns thinking about that resource?

Cooling these data centers requires a lot of water. In places like Saline, there's already a permit application open for river discharge, which has residents asking about quality and quantity impacts.
So this Coldwater meeting feels like a test case for how other communities might handle similar proposals.
It really does. What residents say tonight could influence how planners in nearby townships approach their own reviews.
Any sense of the timeline after tonight?
The council will likely take comments, review the details internally, and then decide on next steps, which could include more public hearings or negotiations with the developers.
And the tax breaks piece — how much of that burden shifts to local taxpayers if the incentives are approved?

That's the trade-off people are debating. The incentives are meant to attract jobs and investment, but critics argue the lost revenue has to be made up somewhere, often through higher property taxes or reduced services.
What kind of jobs are we talking about? Are these high-paying roles or mostly construction work?
The pitch usually includes both construction jobs during the build and ongoing operations roles, but residents want to see the actual numbers and whether those positions go to local workers.
This all sounds familiar from other spots. How many communities are dealing with this right now?
It's heating up across southwest Michigan and beyond, with meetings and permit filings popping up in several counties at the same time.
Do you think tonight's session will set any kind of precedent?
It could. If Coldwater comes out with clear conditions or a pause, other towns might follow the same playbook.
And if it goes smoothly?
Then developers might see a path forward and accelerate plans in other locations that are watching closely.
Either way, it feels like the start of a longer conversation.
Absolutely. We'll be tracking how the feedback shapes the next moves.
Let's shift to some of the other developments from today and yesterday.
Verrus is pushing ahead with a Michigan project even while its Salem plans stay uncertain. Local officials there are already answering questions about power demand and potential tax deals.
Which town might land it? Any hints on size?
Nothing specific yet on the site or scale, but communities across the state are watching to see where the next big facility lands.
That uncertainty is keeping everyone on edge.
On the political side, Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed rallied at the Saline site to criticize AI power deals and tax breaks.
What was his main argument?
He said the grid strain and infrastructure costs would hit Michigan residents while the benefits go elsewhere, and he used the Saline project as the backdrop.
Residents 30 minutes away could see higher electric rates if the campus pulls hundreds of megawatts without new generation.
That's the point he hammered, and it shows how these local projects are now part of the broader Democratic primary conversation ahead of the August vote.
Noise complaints are also shaping the debate. In Dowagiac, neighbors say a constant high-pitched whine from an existing facility runs day and night.
Those complaints are now influencing how Cass County will handle future proposals, with residents pushing for rules that protect sleep and property values.
That kind of real-world impact could change how new projects get approved.
A U.S. representative is also calling for a Commerce Department review of Chinese robots at the Hyperscale Data Michigan site, raising supply-chain security questions.
Could that lead to delays or new federal scrutiny for residents near the project?
It might. Local construction jobs could be affected depending on how the review plays out.
From yesterday, Saline has a river discharge permit application open for public comment tied to a major project.
Residents in Washtenaw County are watching for impacts on water quality and usage, and the filing underscores the ongoing infrastructure tensions.
The District C county council race is also tied to this. Both contenders want to pause large AI projects until power and zoning rules catch up.
They argue local rules aren't ready yet, and the outcome could set the tone for other southwest Michigan townships facing similar proposals.
El-Sayed also slammed the Saline plan on C-SPAN yesterday over power and water costs, saying tax breaks and strain would fall on residents.
That sharpens the debate right before the primary.
And there's an August session coming up where residents can hear power, jobs and tax details on a proposed project.
That gives people a direct chance to ask questions before decisions advance.
A council hopeful in another area wants to halt proposals until rural impacts on power and land are clearer.
Voters will decide whether that protects resources or slows growth.
Plenty to watch. Let's look ahead to meetings listeners can actually attend.
The big one is that August data center session where the project details on power, jobs and taxes will be laid out for the public.
The Saline River discharge permit is also open for comment right now, so residents can weigh in on water impacts.
And the District C race continues to shape the conversation around pauses and zoning studies.
We'll keep you posted on exact dates and locations as they firm up.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Coldwater Residents Get First Look at Data Center Plans as Statewide Scrutiny Grows
